`src/sort.rs` in the fixture (`/home/projects/ulwbench-home/tmp-new/ulw-bench-S6-r1-ox4dJx`) implements quicksort with the Lomuto partition scheme. Its worst case is O(n²) time.

**Source:** `quicksort<T: Ord>` in `src/sort.rs` always picks the last element, `arr[len-1]`, as the pivot. `partition` scans once with `arr[j] <= pivot`, then swaps the pivot into position `i`. It recurses on both sides, with no random or median-of-three pivot.

**Worst case:** O(n²) time. The doc comment in the file says the same. It happens whenever the last element is repeatedly the minimum or maximum of its slice, which leaves one side empty and the other with n−1 elements. That gives about n(n−1)/2 comparisons. Average and best cases are O(n log n).

**Inputs that trigger it:** the comment lists sorted and reverse-sorted input. It misses all-equal input. Because the partition uses `<=`, every element goes to the left side, so an all-equal slice degrades the same way.

**Space:** the worst case also makes the recursion depth O(n). On a large adversarial input that risks a stack overflow, not just slowness.

The fixture's `src/sort.rs` implements **quicksort with the Lomuto partition scheme**. Its worst case is **O(n²) time**.

I read the file in the current working directory, `ulw-bench-S6-r2-EhFuON/src/sort.rs`. It is one 30-line file, so I read it directly instead of running the research swarm. I did not execute it.

**Why it is quicksort with Lomuto partitioning:**
- `quicksort` calls `partition`, then splits the slice at the pivot index and recurses on the left part and on `right[1..]`.
- `partition` always takes the last element as the pivot, `arr[len - 1]`. It scans with `j`, swaps every element `<=` the pivot to the front using `i`, and finally swaps the pivot into position `i`.

**Why the worst case is O(n²):**
- Because the pivot is always the last element, the split is badly unbalanced whenever that element is the minimum or maximum of the slice.
- Already-sorted input makes the pivot the maximum every time. The partition then produces sub-slices of sizes `n-1` and `0`.
- Reverse-sorted input makes the pivot the minimum every time. That gives sizes `0` and `n-1`.
- The recurrence is T(n) = T(n-1) + Θ(n), which sums to Θ(n²).
- Arrays of all equal elements also hit it. The `<=` comparison sends every element to the left side, so the split is `n-1` and `0` again.
- The recursion depth in that case is O(n), so a large sorted input can also overflow the stack.

**Average and best case:** Both are O(n log n), as the file's own doc comment says.

**The doc comment is inaccurate:** It says the worst case happens when elements are "already sorted or reverse sorted with an edge pivot." In this code the pivot is always the last element, so that phrasing is misleading. Sorted input, reverse-sorted input and all-equal input are the worst-case inputs.

**Other copies:** `find` also turned up `sort.rs` in two `tmp-base` fixture directories and in `/tmp/sortverify`. My attempt to diff them against this one printed no usable result (the shell never expanded `$?`), so I haven't confirmed they are identical.

Both parse `+`/`-` integer expressions into an AST. Neither is called from anywhere else in the crate (`lib.rs` only declares the modules) and neither has tests.

|---|---|---|
| Input | raw `&str`, tokenizes inline | pre-tokenized `&[String]` |
| AST | `Expr::{Number, Binary}` | `AstNode::{Val, Op}` |

| Errors | `Err("Expected digit at position N")`, with position | `Err("Malformed token sequence")` / `Err("Empty tokens")`, no position |

| Whitespace | skipped before numbers only | n/a (caller tokenizes) |

## Findings

Findings come from running both parsers on probe inputs in a scratch crate (rustc 1.98.0), with a small evaluator over each AST. The tokenizer for B was `split_whitespace` after padding `+` and `-` with spaces.

1. **B is wrong on chained subtraction.** `10-2-3` gives `Op('-', 10, Op('-', 2, 3))`, which evaluates to 11. A gives `((10-2)-3)`, which is 5. B reduces all operators only after the scan, popping from the end, so every chain is right-associative. `1+2-3` happens to evaluate the same either way.
2. **B is not a real shift-reduce parser.** It never reduces during the scan, and the "table-driven" claim has no table behind it. It has no precedence handling either, which would matter as soon as `*` is added.
3. **B silently drops unknown tokens.** `["1","*","2"]` returns `Ok(Val(2))`, and `1+2x` becomes a "Malformed" error only by accident of token count.
4. **B's "bounded constant stack memory" doc claim is false.** Both `Vec`s grow with input length. Its linear-time claim is fine.
5. **A mishandles spaces and trailing input.** `\
